```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

In finite mixture modelling, the number of latent classes is not known a
priori and is not a parameter of the model; it must be determined by
comparing models fitted with different numbers of classes. No single
statistic identifies the correct number: information criteria,
likelihood-based tests and indices of classification quality each have known
limitations, and they frequently disagree (Nylund, Asparouhov and Muthén,
2007). Class enumeration is therefore an inferential judgement that
integrates several sources of evidence and is reported transparently. This
guide describes each source of evidence that latents computes for a set of
candidate models: its definition, its interpretation, and the conditions
under which it is unreliable. It then outlines how these sources are combined
into a defensible and reproducible decision. A complete applied example is
given in [Class enumeration in mixture models](class-enumeration.html).

The evidence falls into five kinds, each answering a different question.

| Question | Evidence | Verbs |
|---|---|---|
| Which candidate balances fit and size best? | Information criteria and their minima | `as.data.frame()`, `get_results(x, "best")`, `plot(x)` |
| Where do added classes stop paying off? | Changes between neighbouring candidates and the knee of each curve | `get_results(x, "deltas")`, `get_results(x, "knees")`, `plot(x, what = "deltas")`, `plot(x, what = "heatmap")` |
| Are the classes distinct? | Entropy, average posterior probability, odds of correct classification | `get_results(x, "classification")`, `plot(x, what = "diagnostics")` |
| Can the estimate be trusted? | Convergence, boundary estimates, replication of the best likelihood, the smallest class | `plot(x, what = "trust")`, `plot(x, what = "smallest")` |
| Is one more class supported? | The bootstrap likelihood ratio test of neighbouring candidates | `bootstrap_lrt()` |

`plot(x, what = "selection")` draws the plots of the second, third and fourth
rows together, and `compare_models()` places chosen candidates side by side.

```{r setup}
library(latents)
```

## The candidates

The examples use `course_engagement`: course enrolments nested in students,
with five standardized measures of activity per enrolment. Every combination
of one to six profiles and one to four group classes is fitted with a
covariance structure of free variances and zero covariances (`"VVI"`). Three
random starts per candidate keep the example short; applied analyses use ten
or more, because replication of the best likelihood across starts is itself
part of the evidence.

```{r enumerate}
activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
models
```

```{r grid-values, include = FALSE}
candidates <- as.data.frame(models)
n_candidates <- nrow(candidates)
n_fitted <- with(candidates, sum(!is.na(log_likelihood)))
n_students <- with(course_engagement, length(unique(student)))
n_enrolments <- nrow(course_engagement)
```

The grid holds `r n_candidates` candidates, of which `r n_fitted` were
fitted. A candidate with one profile and several group classes is not
identified, because group classes that share a single profile cannot differ,
so it is listed and left unfitted. Every candidate is named by its numbers of
classes, `profiles4_groups3` for four profiles and three group classes, and
the verbs below accept that name.

## Before fitting: starts, scaling and missing values

Three choices are made before any candidate is fitted. Each is passed through
the `...` of `enumerate_classes()`, `enumerate_lpa()` and `enumerate_lca()`,
so every candidate receives the same setting, and each is reported with the
choice of the number of classes.

### Random starts

`n_starts` sets the number of random starts per candidate. More starts make it
less likely that a candidate is reported at a local maximum of its
likelihood, and a candidate stuck at a local maximum usually separates its
classes worse than it would at the global one: refitting with more starts
often raises its entropy and AvePP. The whole grid is refitted with the same,
larger number of starts, not only the candidates of interest; otherwise the
refitted candidates gain likelihood and separation that the others were not
given the chance to reach.

```{r starts, eval = FALSE}
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:6, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            model = "VVI", n_starts = 20, seed = 1)
```

### Centring and scaling

`centering` subtracts a mean and `scaling` divides by a standard deviation,
each at one of two levels: `"grand"` uses one value per indicator over all
observations, and `"person"` one per group. Together they give the classical
z-scores: `centering = "grand", scaling = "grand"` standardizes each indicator
over the sample, and `centering = "person", scaling = "person"` standardizes
it within each group, so the profiles describe how an observation departs
from its own group's usual level and spread.

For the covariance structures that give every indicator its own variance
(`EEI`, `VVI`, `EEE`, `VVV`, `EVI`, `VEI`), grand scaling changes only the
units of the estimates: memberships, entropy and AvePP are unchanged. The
spherical `EII` and `VII` force one variance on every indicator, so an
unscaled indicator with a wide range would dominate the classes; with them,
the indicators are scaled first.

```{r scaling}
srl_indicators <- c("cognitive_strategies", "intrinsic_value",
                    "self_efficacy", "self_regulation", "test_anxiety")
spherical <- enumerate_lpa(srl, srl_indicators, n_profiles = 2:4,
                           model = "EII", centering = "grand",
                           scaling = "grand", n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
get_results(spherical, "best")
```

Scaling moves the log likelihood, so information criteria compare only
candidates fitted with the same centring and scaling, as the candidates of one
grid are.

### Missing values

With `missing = "fiml"`, a row with some indicators missing is fitted from the
indicators it has, and nothing is imputed. A row with every indicator missing
adds nothing to the likelihood, and its posterior is only the prior its group
implies: it was never classified. Such rows are left out of the sample size
of the individual-level criteria and out of entropy, AvePP and the
classification tables, as Mplus leaves them out of its analysis; the fit's
`n_informative` counts the rows that remain, and its print reports how many
were left out. A group whose every row has nothing observed is left out of
the group sample size and the group-level statistics in the same way
(`n_informative_groups`); a group with at least one observed row stays. Rows
with some values missing stay in every statistic: they are classified, less
certainly, from fewer indicators.

```{r missing}
set.seed(3)
incomplete <- course_engagement
empty <- sample(nrow(incomplete), 150)
incomplete[empty, activity] <- NA
partial <- setdiff(sample(nrow(incomplete), 150), empty)
incomplete[partial, "attendance"] <- NA
incomplete_fit <- multilpa(incomplete, activity, "student", n_profiles = 3,
                           n_group_classes = 2, model = "VVI",
                           missing = "fiml", n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
get_results(incomplete_fit, "entropy")
```

```{r missing-values, include = FALSE}
incomplete_entropy <- get_results(incomplete_fit, "entropy")
classified_rows <- with(subset(incomplete_entropy, level == "individuals"),
                        n_units)
stopifnot(classified_rows == nrow(incomplete) - length(empty))
```

The entropy of the individuals is taken over `r classified_rows` rows: the
`r format(nrow(incomplete), big.mark = ",")` enrolments less the
`r length(empty)` with nothing observed. Dropping those rows from the data by
hand gives the same estimates, likelihood and classification statistics;
dropping rows with only some values missing would change the sample and, if
their missingness depends on what was observed, bias the profiles.

## Information criteria

### Definitions

Each criterion starts from the deviance, `-2L`, where `L` is the maximized
log likelihood, and adds a charge. With `q` free parameters, `n` the sample
size and `EN` the classification entropy, `EN = -sum(p log p)` summed over
every unit and class of the posterior probabilities `p`:

| Criterion | Formula | Charge depends on | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| `aic` | `-2L + 2q` | parameters only | Akaike (1974) |
| `kic` | `-2L + 3(q + 1)` | parameters only | Cavanaugh (1999) |
| `bic` | `-2L + q log(n)` | sample size | Schwarz (1978) |
| `sabic` | `-2L + q log((n + 2) / 24)` | sample size | Sclove (1987) |
| `caic` | `-2L + q (log(n) + 1)` | sample size | Bozdogan (1987) |
| `icl` | `-2L + q log(n) + 2 EN` | sample size and classification | Biernacki, Celeux and Govaert (2000) |
| `awe` | `-2(L - EN) + 2q (1.5 + log(n))` | sample size and classification | Banfield and Raftery (1993) |
| `clc` | `-2L + 2 EN` | classification only | Biernacki and Govaert (1997) |

Lower is better for every criterion. The charge per parameter is 2 for AIC,
3 for KIC, `log((n + 2) / 24)` for SABIC, `log(n)` for BIC and
`log(n) + 1` for CAIC, so above a few dozen units AIC is the most lenient and
CAIC the strictest of these, and a larger charge favours fewer classes. ICL
and AWE add a charge for classification uncertainty, because a class that
overlaps its neighbours raises `EN`, and so favour fewer and better
separated classes than BIC. CLC has no charge per parameter, only the
entropy charge, so it can favour many classes when they are well separated
and few when they are not. CLC uses the entropy sum as ICL and AWE do. Some software reports a CLC built
from relative entropy, which is bounded by one and charges almost nothing,
and the two numbers are not comparable.

### Two conventions for the sample size

In a two-level model the sample size is either the number of groups, here
the `r n_students` students, or the number of observations, the
`r format(n_enrolments, big.mark = ",")` enrolments. latents reports every
criterion that depends on a sample size under both conventions: the columns
ending `_groups` count groups and use the posterior probabilities of the
group classes for `EN`, and the columns ending `_individual` count
observations and use the posterior probabilities of the profiles. Neither is
the definition of a multilevel BIC; they are two stated choices, and an
analysis picks one and keeps it for every candidate. AIC and KIC have no
sample size and carry no convention.

In a single-level grid there are no groups, the two sample sizes coincide,
and BIC, SABIC and CAIC are the same under both conventions. The entropy
criteria are not: their `_groups` columns use the classification of the
group classes, of which a single-level model has one, so they carry no
classification charge and ICL there equals BIC. In a single-level grid, read
the `_individual` columns of ICL, AWE and CLC.

### The table of every candidate

`as.data.frame()` returns one row per candidate with every criterion under
both conventions, beside its log likelihood, number of parameters,
classification summaries and estimation checks.

```{r candidates}
as.data.frame(models)
```

### The minimum of each criterion

`get_results(x, "best")` reduces that table to one row per criterion and
convention: the candidate at the criterion's minimum, its numbers of
classes and the minimum value. It answers "which candidate does each
criterion favour?" and nothing more.

```{r best}
get_results(models, "best")
```

```{r best-values, include = FALSE}
best <- get_results(models, "best")
pick <- function(name, convention_name) {
  with(subset(best, criterion == name & convention %in% convention_name),
       candidate)
}
bic_groups_pick <- pick("bic", "groups")
bic_individual_pick <- pick("bic", "individuals")
icl_groups_pick <- pick("icl", "groups")
aic_pick <- with(subset(best, criterion == "aic"), candidate)
n_distinct_picks <- length(unique(best$candidate))
largest <- with(subset(candidates, !is.na(log_likelihood)),
                sprintf("profiles%d_groups%d", max(n_profiles),
                        max(n_group_classes)))
```

Here the criteria name `r n_distinct_picks` different candidates. BIC with
students as the units favours `r bic_groups_pick`, BIC with enrolments
`r bic_individual_pick`, ICL with students `r icl_groups_pick`, and AIC
`r aic_pick`. Disagreement is the usual outcome, not a failure: the
criteria were built for different purposes, and the size of their charges
explains much of the disagreement: AIC, with the lightest charge, names the
largest candidate, and the entropy criteria name smaller ones.

A minimum on the edge of the grid, at the largest number of profiles or
group classes fitted, means the criterion was still falling there. Such a
minimum says only that the range was too narrow. The range is widened until
the minimum lies inside it, or, when the criterion keeps falling at every
size the data can support, the size of each decrease becomes the evidence,
as in the next section.

### Plotting the criteria

`plot()` draws the criteria against the number of profiles, one line per
number of group classes, and rings the lowest value of each. `what` names
criteria by their columns, and `what = "all"` draws every one.

```{r plot-criteria, fig.height = 5}
plot(models)
```

```{r plot-bic}
plot(models, what = "bic_groups")
```

## Where added classes stop paying off

### Deltas

When a criterion falls across the whole range, its minimum carries little
information, but the size of each fall does. `get_results(x, "deltas")`
reports, for every candidate, the decrease in a criterion from its neighbour
with one profile fewer (`delta_profile`, from `from_profile`) and from its
neighbour with one group class fewer (`delta_group_class`, from
`from_group_class`). A positive delta means the added class lowered the
criterion; a negative delta means it raised it. A candidate with no such
neighbour in the grid has `NA`. The criterion is BIC with groups as the
units unless `using` names another column.

```{r deltas}
get_results(models, "deltas")
```

```{r deltas-values, include = FALSE}
deltas <- get_results(models, "deltas")
delta_of <- function(name) with(subset(deltas, candidate == name),
                                round(delta_profile))
step_3 <- delta_of("profiles3_groups3")
step_4 <- delta_of("profiles4_groups3")
step_5 <- delta_of("profiles5_groups3")
stopifnot(step_3 > step_4, step_4 > 0, step_5 < 0)
```

With three group classes, the third profile lowers BIC by
`r format(step_3, big.mark = ",")` and the fourth by
`r format(step_4, big.mark = ",")`, and the fifth raises it by
`r format(-step_5, big.mark = ",")`, which the table shows as a negative
decrease. The candidate with two profiles has no delta along the profiles,
because its neighbour with one profile and three group classes is not
identified. Shrinking falls mark the point after which further profiles add
detail rather than structure, and the first negative delta marks where they
stop improving the criterion at all. The deltas are plotted for both directions, along the number of
profiles on the left and along the number of group classes on the right.

```{r plot-deltas, fig.height = 5}
plot(models, what = "deltas")
```

Any criterion can be read this way:

```{r plot-deltas-icl, fig.height = 5}
plot(models, what = "deltas", using = "icl_individual")
```

### Knees

The knee, or elbow, is where a falling curve bends from steep to flat.
`get_results(x, "knees")` locates it by a rule inspired by Kneedle
(Satopää, Albrecht, Irwin and Raghavan, 2011), simplified to its geometric
core:

1. both axes of the curve, the number of classes and the criterion, are
   rescaled to the unit interval;
2. a straight line is drawn from the first candidate to the last;
3. the knee is the candidate furthest below that line, measured
   perpendicular to it, and `distance` is that perpendicular distance in the
   rescaled units.

Kneedle's smoothing and sensitivity thresholds are left out, so a nearly
straight curve can still name a knee with a very small `distance`. The
distance therefore reports the strength of the bend as well as its place. A
curve whose last value is not below its first has no knee, because a bend in
a rising criterion marks no diminishing return.

Knees are found along three kinds of line: along the number of profiles at
each number of group classes (`direction = "profiles"`), along the number of
group classes at each number of profiles (`"group_classes"`), and across all
candidates ordered by their number of parameters (`"parameters"`). The
columns `from` and `to` give the ends of the line and `n_points` its length.

```{r knees}
get_results(models, "knees")
```

The straight line ends at the largest candidate fitted, so the knee depends
on where the grid stops: fitting one more candidate moves the line and can
move the knee. The table tests that directly. `knee_without_largest` is the
knee of the same line with its last candidate removed, and `stable` is
`TRUE` when the two agree. A knee that moves when the range shrinks by one
candidate is weak evidence. `note` explains every row without a full
answer:

| `note` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| empty | a knee was found and is stable |
| `fewer than three candidates` | a line needs three points for a knee |
| `three candidates: stability not assessed` | `stable` needs four points |
| `the criterion does not fall along this line` | no diminishing return to find |
| `the curve does not bend below the line` | the curve is straight or bends upward |
| `no knee when the largest is left out` | the shortened line has no knee |
| `moves when the largest is left out` | the knee depends on the range fitted |

```{r knee-values, include = FALSE}
knees <- get_results(models, "knees")
profile_line <- subset(knees, direction == "profiles" &
                         line == "3 group classes")
knee_three <- with(profile_line, knee_candidate)
knee_three_without <- with(profile_line, knee_without_largest)
knee_three_distance <- with(profile_line, round(distance, 2))
knee_three_stable <- with(profile_line, stable)
```

With three group classes, the knee along the number of profiles is
`r knee_three` at a distance of `r knee_three_distance`. Without the largest
candidate it is `r knee_three_without`, so `stable` is
`r knee_three_stable`: the bend lies between three and four profiles, and
which of the two the rule names depends on where the grid stops. The deltas
locate the same region with less ambiguity, which is why the two are read
together.

### The criterion over the whole grid

The heatmap shows every candidate at once, coloured by how far its criterion
lies above the lowest value in the grid. It reads the same criterion as the
deltas and takes the same `using`.

```{r heatmap}
plot(models, what = "heatmap")
```

## Are the classes distinct?

A candidate can fit well and still separate its classes poorly, leaving many
units between classes and their assignments uncertain. Three statistics
describe the separation, each from the posterior probabilities of
membership.

- **Relative entropy**, `1 - EN / (n log K)` for `K` classes, runs from 0,
  every unit equally likely to belong to every class, to 1, every unit
  certain. It summarizes a whole level in one number and is `NA` for a level
  with one class, where it is undefined rather than perfect.
- **Average posterior probability (AvePP)** of a class is the mean posterior
  probability of that class among the units assigned to it. Values of 0.7 to
  0.8 and above are commonly read as adequate separation (Nagin, 2005). It
  is reported per class, so a single poorly separated class is visible
  where entropy would average it away.
- **Odds of correct classification (OCC)** of a class is
  `(p / (1 - p)) / (r / (1 - r))`, with `p` its AvePP and `r` its estimated
  share. It compares classification against a guess from the class size
  alone: near 1 is no better than the guess, and 5 or more is the usual
  floor for adequate separation (Nagin, 2005).

The table of candidates summarizes each level by its relative entropy and the
smallest, largest and mean AvePP, and counts the classes below a cutoff of
0.8, set with `cutoff`. `get_results(x, "classification")` gives every class
of every candidate: its size by modal assignment and by estimate, its AvePP,
its OCC and the relative entropy of its level.

```{r classification}
get_results(models, "classification")
```

`plot(x, what = "diagnostics")` draws relative entropy and the lowest AvePP
across the candidates, with the cutoff dashed; `what = "entropy"` and
`what = "avepp"` draw one of the two. For one fitted candidate,
`plot_diagnostics()` draws the certainty of every unit in its class, the
uncertainty of every unit, the class sizes and the average posterior
matrix, for the profiles and, when there are two or more group classes, for
the group classes (`what = "group_posteriors"` and the like). The two levels
often differ sharply: a group is classified from all of its observations
together, and an observation from its own responses alone.

```{r diagnostics}
plot(models, what = "diagnostics")
```

Entropy and AvePP can disagree, and the difference is informative. AvePP
reads only the posterior of each unit's assigned class; entropy reads the
whole row of posteriors. A unit at 0.70 for its class and 0.10 for each of
three others, and a unit at 0.70 and 0.30, give the same AvePP, but the first,
spread over every class, lowers entropy much more. Entropy also falls faster
for a few very uncertain units than it rises for many certain ones. A level
with most units near certainty and a tail of uncertain ones therefore shows a
moderate AvePP beside a low entropy.

The two levels of a two-level model are classified from different amounts of
information. A group class is assigned from all of a group's observations
together, an observation's profile from its own responses alone, so group
classes are usually much sharper. For one candidate, `plot_diagnostics()`
draws both levels:

```{r group-certainty}
plot_diagnostics(get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3"),
                 what = "group_posteriors")
```

When every candidate separates its profiles poorly, so that no number of
classes brings entropy or the smallest AvePP up, the indicators do not
separate single observations well, and the number of classes is chosen from
the criteria and the interpretation, with the separation reported as a
limitation. Modal assignments are then a poor substitute for the classes in
a later analysis, and the bias-corrected three-step estimates (`r3step()`,
`three_step()`) are used instead.

Classification quality is not a criterion for the number of classes in
itself: a model with fewer classes is usually better separated, so choosing
by entropy alone favours too few classes. It decides between candidates that
the criteria leave close, and it qualifies how the chosen classes can be
used, for instance whether modal assignments can stand in for the classes in
a later analysis.

## Can the estimate be trusted?

### Estimation checks

The likelihood of a mixture model has several local maxima. A solution
reached from several random starts is more credible than one reached once,
and an estimate on the boundary of the parameter space, a variance at its
floor or a class with almost no members, marks a model too complex for the
data. `plot(x, what = "trust")` gives each candidate one tile, labelled with
the number of starts that reached its best log likelihood, and coloured by
the first problem it has:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| best replicated | converged, inside the parameter space, best likelihood reached by more than one start |
| best found once | as above, but only one start reached the best likelihood |
| on a boundary | an estimate reached the edge of the parameter space |
| not converged | the EM algorithm stopped before meeting its tolerance |
| not fitted (`x`) | not identified, or failed with an error kept in the table |

```{r trust}
plot(models, what = "trust")
```

A candidate found once is refitted with more starts before it is chosen, and
so is the rest of the grid (see *Random starts* above). If the refit raises its
likelihood, the earlier solution was a local maximum and the new one replaces
it; its entropy and AvePP often rise with it. A higher AvePP is never a
reason to prefer one solution over another of the same candidate: the
solution with the higher likelihood is the estimate. The columns
`converged`, `boundary`, `n_best_replicated`, `warnings` and `error` of the
table of candidates hold the same checks.

### The smallest class

A class holding a very small share of the units is hard to interpret and
estimated from little data. `plot(x, what = "smallest")` draws the estimated
share of the smallest class of every candidate, with a dashed line at 5%, a
common floor rather than a rule.

```{r smallest}
plot(models, what = "smallest")
```

## All of the plots together

`plot(x, what = "selection")` returns the deltas, the heatmap, the smallest
class, the estimation checks and the classification diagnostics as one list
of plots, drawn in turn. `using` sets the criterion of the first two and
`cutoff` the AvePP line of the last.

```{r selection, fig.height = 5}
plot(models, what = "selection")
```

## How the profiles divide

The tree shows how the profiles of each model divide into those of the next:
each profile is linked to the profiles of the model with one more that
receive its observations (Zappia and Oshlack, 2018). A profile that splits
cleanly in two suggests a real distinction; one that draws from several
profiles of the smaller model suggests a reshuffling.

```{r tree, fig.height = 6}
plot(models, what = "tree")
```

## Comparing chosen candidates

Once the evidence narrows the choice to a few candidates,
`compare_models()` places them side by side, named or by their numbers of
classes. Its table adds the difference of each candidate's BIC from the
lowest among those compared, `delta_bic`, and its BIC weight,
`exp(-delta_bic / 2)` normalized over the compared candidates: the
approximate posterior probability of each if one of them is true and all
were equally likely beforehand (Wagenmakers and Farrell, 2004). The weights
depend on which candidates are compared.

```{r compare}
comparison <- compare_models(models, "profiles3_groups3", "profiles4_groups3",
                             "profiles4_groups2")
comparison
plot(comparison)
```

The model behind a row is taken out with `get_candidate()`, by name or by
numbers of classes.

```{r chosen}
chosen <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
chosen
```

## Testing one more class

The usual likelihood ratio test is invalid between mixtures with `k` and
`k + 1` classes, because the smaller model sits on the boundary of the
larger one, where the statistic loses its reference distribution.
`bootstrap_lrt()` simulates that distribution (McLachlan, 1987; Nylund,
Asparouhov and Muthén, 2007): data sets are drawn from the smaller fitted
model, both models are refitted to each, and the observed statistic is
placed among the simulated ones. With `B` simulated data sets and `b`
statistics at least as large as the observed one, the p-value is
`(b + 1) / (B + 1)`, which can never be zero and cannot fall below
`1 / (B + 1)`. A replicate that fails a fitting check withholds the p-value
rather than drop silently. The example uses 19 data sets, whose smallest
attainable p-value is 0.05; applied analyses use 99 or more.

```{r blrt}
smaller <- get_candidate(models, "profiles3_groups3")
larger <- get_candidate(models, "profiles4_groups3")
test <- bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data = course_engagement,
                      iter = 19, n_starts = 2, seed = 1)
test
plot(test)
```

## Putting the evidence together

No rule turns this evidence into a number of classes, and latents does not
apply one. A choice is made by reading the evidence in a fixed order and
reporting every step:

0. **State the preparation**: the number of starts, any centring and
   scaling, and how missing values were handled, with how many rows had
   nothing observed.
1. **State the convention** for the sample size before reading any
   criterion, and keep it.
2. **Read the minima** of the criteria under that convention. Note where
   they agree and in which direction they disagree. A minimum on the edge of
   the grid calls for a wider grid.
3. **Read the deltas and knees** when the criteria keep falling. Report the
   knee with its `distance` and whether it is `stable`.
4. **Check classification** of the candidates still in contention: relative
   entropy, the smallest AvePP and OCC of each level.
5. **Check estimation**: replication of the best likelihood, boundary
   estimates and the smallest class. Refit a candidate found once with more
   starts.
6. **Test** the leading candidate against its neighbour with the bootstrap
   likelihood ratio test when the evidence is close.
7. **Interpret** the leading candidates. Between candidates that the
   statistics leave close, the one whose classes are distinct and
   meaningful for the question is chosen, and the reason is stated.

The tables behind every step are returned by the verbs above, so the
reported choice can be reproduced from the reported evidence.

## Functions

```{r reference, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Call = c(
    "enumerate_classes(..., n_starts = , centering = , scaling = , missing = \"fiml\")",
    "as.data.frame(models)",
    "get_results(models, \"best\")",
    "plot(models), plot(models, what = \"bic_groups\"), what = \"all\"",
    "get_results(models, \"deltas\", using = )",
    "plot(models, what = \"deltas\", using = )",
    "get_results(models, \"knees\", using = )",
    "plot(models, what = \"heatmap\", using = )",
    "get_results(models, \"classification\")",
    "get_results(models, \"candidates\", cutoff = )",
    "plot(models, what = \"diagnostics\", \"entropy\" or \"avepp\", cutoff = )",
    "get_results(fit, \"entropy\")",
    "plot_diagnostics(fit), what = \"group_posteriors\" and the like",
    "plot(models, what = \"trust\")",
    "plot(models, what = \"smallest\")",
    "plot(models, what = \"selection\")",
    "plot(models, what = \"tree\")",
    "compare_models(models, \"name\", ...)",
    "get_candidate(models, \"name\")",
    "bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data, iter)"),
  Result = c(
    "The same starts, centring, scaling and missing-data handling for every candidate",
    "One row per candidate: every criterion, classification summaries and checks",
    "The candidate at the minimum of each criterion and convention",
    "Criteria across the candidates, lowest ringed",
    "Decrease in a criterion from one profile fewer and one group class fewer",
    "The decreases along profiles and along group classes",
    "Chord-distance knee of each line, with its stability",
    "Distance of every candidate from the lowest criterion",
    "Size, AvePP, OCC and entropy of every class of every candidate",
    "The table of candidates with another AvePP cutoff",
    "Relative entropy and lowest AvePP across the candidates",
    "Relative entropy of one fit at each level, over the classified units",
    "Certainty, uncertainty, sizes and AvePP of one fit, profiles and group classes",
    "Convergence, boundary and replication of every candidate",
    "Share of the smallest class of every candidate",
    "Deltas, heatmap, smallest class, trust and diagnostics together",
    "How the profiles divide as more are added",
    "Chosen candidates side by side, with BIC weights",
    "One fitted candidate",
    "Bootstrap likelihood ratio test of k against k + 1 classes")),
  col.names = c("Call", "Result"))
```
